data.title: New Jersey Man Sentenced to 63 Months for Defrauding Elderly Victims of $1,130,406
data.description:
Federal prosecutors have secured a 63-month prison sentence against a New Jersey man who stole more than $1 million from elderly victims by falsely promising to invest their money.

Antonio Petrosino, 61, of Union City, New Jersey, received the term on November 5th, 2026, from U.S. District Judge Stanley R. Chesler after pleading guilty to wire fraud on March 25, 2026, says the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of New Jersey.

The scheme ran from January 2016 through November 2024 and involved tricking victims into sending money for supposed investments or personal benefit.

Petrosino presented fake investment statements to one elderly victim, showing hundreds of thousands of dollars in accounts, and gave false assurances when questioned about the funds.

“As part of the scheme, Petrosino held himself out to be a financial services professional and falsely led his victims to believe that he would invest their money in brokerage accounts and other investment products or otherwise use it for their benefit… In reality, Petrosino failed to invest the victims’ funds or otherwise use victim monies for the victims’ benefit.”

He spent the money on personal expenses such as gambling, credit card bills, and rent for a luxury apartment instead of making any investments.

The total amount taken reached approximately $1.1 million.

Judge Chesler also imposed two years of supervised release along with forfeiture and restitution totaling $1,130,406.63.

The FBI, Federal Reserve Board Office of Inspector General, and Wyckoff Police Department conducted the investigation.

data.title: Indiana Ex-Letter Carrier Gets 6.5 Years in Prison for $34,000,000 Check Theft Scheme
data.description:
Federal authorities have sentenced a former postal worker to six and a half years in prison after she stole thousands of checks from the mail as part of a widespread fraud operation.

Destinee Ruffin, 29, of Indianapolis, pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit bank fraud and theft of mail, says the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of Indiana.

Agents found thousands of unsold stolen checks worth more than $20 million hidden in her home and vehicle during a 2024 search.

Ruffin supplied over $12 million in checks to one co-conspirator and more than $235,000 to another, who then altered and deposited them.

“Ruffin was employed as a letter carrier at the Bacon Station Post Office. Between April 2020 and May 2022, Ruffin used access to both incoming and outgoing mail to steal checks, which she then sold to co-conspirators.

In spring 2020, as the federal government issued Economic Impact Payment (EIP) checks to taxpayers, the U.S. Postal Service Office of Inspector General (USPS OIG) received a complaint from a Bacon Station customer who never received theirs. Additional complaints soon followed. When agents reviewed the affected addresses and matched them to delivery routes, they discovered all missing checks were assigned to the same mail carrier, Destinee Ruffin.”

The scheme affected about 6,500 victims, including one whose stolen health insurance payment led to a canceled surgery for her husband.

Says Tom Wheeler, United States Attorney for the Southern District of Indiana,

“Destinee Ruffin’s crimes were not isolated acts of theft; they represented a sweeping scheme that touched thousands of households and eroded a fundamental public trust. By stealing millions of dollars’ worth of checks from the mail, Ruffin and her co-conspirators disrupted critical benefits, jeopardized family finances, and caused real harm to individuals who depended on timely delivery for essential needs.”

Three co-conspirators have already been sentenced, while the final defendant faces court on December 3rd, 2026.

data.title: Scammers Spoof Financial Institution’s Real Phone Number, Drain $7,000+ From Connecticut Woman’s Account Through Apple Cash: Report
data.description:
A Connecticut woman has lost over $7,000 after scammers spoofed her credit union’s real phone number and talked her into sending her savings through Apple Cash.

The 45-year-old Windsor resident, who asked not to be named, says the caller claimed to work in the fraud department at 360 Federal Credit Union, reports NBC Connecticut.

She says her caller ID showed the credit union’s name, and the caller told her that her banking information had been compromised and her accounts needed to be secured.

Because her credit union is small, she says the fact that he knew where she banked made him seem like someone trying to help.

The report says that over a weekend in August, she sent more than $7,000 through Apple Cash to an unknown account, believing she was following her credit union’s instructions.

A fraud warning appeared while she was making the payment, but she says the caller told her the alert was a good sign.

“He goes, ‘Good, good. That’s what we want to see. We’re locking everything down.'”

By the following Monday, her account balance had gone negative.

Says the woman,

“All of a sudden it’s just like, whoa, where’s my money?… This person was very calculated. This definitely was not their first time at all.”

360 Federal Credit Union says it has found no sign that the transaction came from a breach of its systems.

She reached out to Apple and Green Dot Bank, which provides Apple Cash services, but has not been able to recover the money.

data.title: New York Man Steals $141,968 in Pension Payments Meant for Deceased Elderly Neighbor for Over Three Years
data.description:
A New York man who served as caretaker for his elderly neighbor has admitted to stealing nearly $142,000 in pension payments that kept flowing after the neighbor died.

Danilo Pesce, 60, of Pelham pleaded guilty to fourth-degree grand larceny in Albany County Court, New York Attorney General Letitia James says.

The neighbor, Jack Lee Morgan, was a retired Pelham school district teacher who collected a pension from the New York State Teachers’ Retirement System.

Morgan died in 2020 with no living beneficiary, so the payments should have stopped.

But nobody told the retirement system about the death, and it kept sending $3,497 a month into Morgan’s bank account.

While working as Morgan’s caretaker, Pesce had been added to the bank account and to the deed of Morgan’s Pelham home.

Starting on March 17th, 2020, less than a month after Morgan died, Pesce regularly pulled money out of the account, the attorney general’s office says.

He used the cash on upkeep and renovations at Morgan’s home, where he and his wife were living part-time.

In total, Pesce took $141,968.

He has paid $147,000 back to the retirement system, which includes $6,000 in interest.

Says James,

“Danilo Pesce took advantage of the retirement system that thousands of hard-working New York teachers rely on… This heartless theft should serve as a reminder that my office will not tolerate anyone who breaks the law to steal from their neighbors.”

Pesce was arrested on July 30th of this year.

data.title: Binance and Polymarket Propose Polygon Hard Fork To Recover About $6,500,000 in Hacked Crypto
data.description:
Crypto exchange giant Binance and prediction markets platform Polymarket want the Polygon (POL) network to move about 70 million tokens out of the hands of the hackers who stole them late last month.

The two firms have filed a Polygon Improvement Proposal for a one-time hard fork that would set the POL balances in five attacker-controlled addresses to zero and credit the same amounts to recovery wallets the companies control, the proposal says.

The five addresses hold about 70.49 million POL, worth roughly $6.5 million at the October 29th price used in the proposal.

About 23.86 million POL sits in four addresses tied to the Polymarket hack on October 29th, while about 46.63 million POL sits in one address tied to the Binance hack that hit late the same day.

Polygon’s block producers have already added the addresses to a block list, so the funds cannot move.

But the companies say that is only a stopgap.

“The funds cannot move, but nothing in the current setup lets them be returned either.”

The proposal says the attacker has kept trying to get the funds out, including by offering validators cash to help unblock a transaction.

The fork would leave Polygon’s total supply unchanged.

It would only go live after approval through Polygon’s governance process, a test run on the Amoy testnet and proof that Binance and Polymarket control the recovery wallets.

The firms call it an extreme action that should not be reproduced commonly.

The plan is set to be presented at the Polygon Protocol Governance Call on November 5th at 14:30 UTC, with rollout expected to take about two weeks after approval.

Binance says it has already replaced most of the roughly $6.3 billion stolen from its hot wallets in the October 29th attack.

data.title: Global Central Banks Splurge $42,423,360,000 on Gold in Just Three Months Amid Heightened ‘Geopolitical Risk and Concerns’
data.description:
Global central banks have added more gold to their reserves in the third quarter than in any quarter since late 2024, according to the World Gold Council, an industry body.

Central banks and other official institutions bought a net 321 tonnes of gold from July through September, up 42% from a year earlier, the World Gold Council says.

The council says portfolio diversification and risk management remain the main reasons behind the buying.

Central bank purchases so far this year stand at 675 tonnes, 6% higher than over the same stretch last year.

Gold-backed exchange-traded funds (ETFs) also returned to inflows, adding 211 tonnes and lifting total holdings to a record 4,256 tonnes.

Total gold demand slipped 1% from a year earlier to 1,369 tonnes, but its value jumped 22% to $188 billion as the gold price averaged $4,262 per ounce.

Demand for gold bars and coins fell 19% to 268 tonnes, while jewelry demand dropped 17% to 313 tonnes, the weakest third quarter in the council’s records.

Technology demand rose 3% to 85 tonnes, its highest quarterly total since late 2021, as AI-related manufacturing lifted electronics demand.

Says Louise Street, senior markets analyst at the World Gold Council,

“The third quarter was a mixed bag for gold demand. Gold ETF inflows came roaring back, with geopolitical risk and concerns around fiscal discipline driving institutional interest, in contrast to retail investors who held back amid uncertainty over the gold price outlook. Central Banks remained an important pillar of demand as pronounced buying continued from the official sector…

The outlook for gold looks finely balanced through to the end of the year. While rising interest rates and mixed inflation expectations present potential headwinds, the combined shadows of geopolitical risk and financial market stress may cause participants to seek stability in gold.”

Gold is trading at $4,130 an ounce at time of writing.

data.title: USPS Insider Who Stole Checks in $34,000,000 Fraud Scheme Hitting About 6,500 Victims Gets Six and a Half Years in Prison
data.description:
A former Indiana letter carrier has been sentenced to six and a half years in federal prison for stealing checks from the mail in a $34 million bank fraud scheme that hit about 6,500 victims.

The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of Indiana says Destinee Ruffin, 29, of Indianapolis also got two years of supervised release after pleading guilty to conspiracy to commit bank fraud and theft of mail.

Ruffin worked at the Bacon Station Post Office in Indianapolis, where she took checks from incoming and outgoing mail between April of 2020 and May of 2022 and sold them to co-conspirators.

The buyers changed the payee names and ran the checks through the bank accounts of people who handed over debit cards, PINs or online banking logins.

Ruffin supplied John Young, 24, with more than $12 million in stolen checks and sold Tony McMullen, 36, more than $235,000 worth.

The case began in the spring of 2020 when a Bacon Station customer complained that an Economic Impact Payment check never arrived, and more complaints led agents to Ruffin’s route.

Investigators later mailed controlled Treasury checks with recorded serial numbers and traced them back to her.

A search of her home, vehicle and devices in April of 2024 turned up thousands of unsold stolen checks worth more than $20 million, with stolen mail piled in closets, in corners and even in the bathroom.

One victim found out her $1,618 payment to keep her retired husband’s health insurance never arrived when she showed up for surgery and was told her coverage had been terminated, forcing the procedure to be canceled.

Says U.S. Attorney Tom Wheeler,

“Destinee Ruffin’s crimes were not isolated acts of theft; they represented a sweeping scheme that touched thousands of households and eroded a fundamental public trust. By stealing millions of dollars’ worth of checks from the mail, Ruffin and her co-conspirators disrupted critical benefits, jeopardized family finances, and caused real harm to individuals who depended on timely delivery for essential needs.”

Ruffin was also ordered to pay $121,270.30 in restitution.

Three of her co-conspirators have already been sentenced, and Young is set to be sentenced on December 3rd.

The Daily Hodl reported on Ruffin’s guilty plea in October.

data.title: Wisconsin School District Loses $450,000 to Bank Impersonation Scam
data.description:
A Wisconsin school district has lost hundreds of thousands of dollars to a bank impersonation scam.

Milwaukee Public Schools (MPS) initially lost $450,000 but has recovered $255,000 and is working to get back the remaining $195,000, reports FOX6 Milwaukee.

The district says it learned it was the victim of bank impersonation fraud and notified authorities on Monday.

MPS has not released details on how or when the fraud happened.

Says MPS Superintendent Brenda Cassellius,

“This is a sobering reminder of the sophisticated financial scams that occur every day across the country. We are taking swift and immediate action to strengthen our internal procedures to prevent this from happening…

We also are working with our partners at US Bank to recover the remainder of the funds.”

The district says it is putting short-term and long-term controls in place to protect its finances, but it has not said what those controls include.

Along with the criminal investigation, MPS is running its own internal probe.

Deputy chief financial officer Jennifer Buros will serve as acting chief financial officer, with help from Charles Burbridge of the Council of the Great City Schools.

The $450,000 loss is less than one-tenth of one percent of the $1.6 billion budget the Milwaukee Board of School Directors approved in May for the 2026-27 school year.

data.title: 3M To Pay $7,350,000,000 To Settle Injury Claims Over ‘Forever Chemicals’ in Firefighting Foam
data.description:
Manufacturing giant 3M has agreed to pay billions of dollars to resolve most of the personal injury claims tied to “forever chemicals” in firefighting foam.

The company says it will make a $7.35 billion commitment over nine years, with a present value of $5.8 billion, to settle claims in the Aqueous Film-Forming Foam (AFFF) multidistrict litigation in South Carolina federal court.

Forever chemicals, known as PFAS, linger in the environment instead of breaking down and have been linked to health problems including cancer, reports The Hill.

3M says the deal addresses about 99% of current personal injury claims inside and outside the multidistrict litigation and involves about 115,000 to 120,000 eligible plaintiffs.

The company will pay $50 million in 2026 and nothing in 2027, with about 20% of the payments due in the final two years.

The total also includes a $680 million reserve fund for remaining and future claims.

Says 3M chairman and CEO William Brown,

“This settlement is a significant milestone for 3M and substantially reduces litigation uncertainty. Following our 2023 resolution with U.S. public water suppliers and our more recent settlement with the State of New Jersey, this is another important step in managing legacy PFAS matters.”

3M denies liability for the PFAS claims and says the agreement is not an admission of liability.

Attorneys Fred Thompson and David Hoyle of the law firm Motley Rice say in a statement,

“For the thousands of victims who have sought answers and accountability for nearly a decade, 3M’s $7.35 billion settlement is welcome news.”

3M separately settled claims from public water systems for more than $10 billion in 2023.

data.title: Washington Resident Pleads Guilty to Wire Fraud in $333,249 Romance Scam
data.description:
Federal prosecutors have secured a guilty plea from a Washington resident accused of running a years-long romance scam that drained over $333,000 from a Portland victim.

Rithy Ham, 45, of Vancouver, Washington, pleaded guilty to one count of wire fraud and one count of money laundering, says the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Oregon.

The scheme ran from September 2020 through May 2024 and relied on invented identities of two women who supposedly needed cash for daily bills, nursing school costs and escape from sex trafficking.

“Believing the women were real and in danger, the victim sent money on multiple occasions.”

The victim sent repeated payments after receiving messages from both Ham and the fabricated profiles.

One transfer of $36,872.35 occurred in November 2022, and another $20,922 came from a retirement account in March 2023.

Ham and his wife controlled the accounts that received the funds, and part of the proceeds paid for an $18,500 check to his wife.

“In total, Ham stole $333,249.52 from the victim, much of it from the victim’s retirement savings.”

Under the plea deal, Ham must repay the full amount and faces up to 20 years in prison on the wire fraud charge and up to 10 years on the money laundering count.

The FBI conducted the investigation.
